questions.question: In a PLONKish/Halo2-style circuit, what does it mean for a gate constraint to be satisfied on a row?
options: Its expression evaluates to 0 in the circuit’s finite field on that row
Its expression evaluates to a positive integer on that row
The prover assigns the same value to every advice cell on that row
The verifier recomputes the witness values from the public inputs
questions.explanation: Gates are algebraic identities over a field; they are satisfied when the evaluated expression is 0.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a selector in Halo2?
options: Conditionally enable a gate on specific rows by multiplying the gate by 0/1
Encrypt the witness values before committing to them
Turn private inputs into public inputs
Reduce the number of columns by hashing them together
questions.explanation: Selectors act like per-row on/off switches for constraints: q(row) * t(row) = 0.

questions.question: Why do many Halo2 gates use the pattern q(row) * t(row) = 0 instead of just t(row) = 0 everywhere?
options: So the same columns can be reused for multiple gadgets, with constraints enabled only where needed
So the prover can choose whether to satisfy the constraint
So the verifier does not need to know the field modulus
So constraints can refer to unlimited numbers of rows at once
questions.explanation: Selectors let you reuse the same columns while only enforcing a gate on the rows where that gadget is laid out.

questions.question: What does an equality (copy) constraint enforce in a Halo2 circuit?
options: Two specified cells must contain the same field element value
Two columns must have the same number of assigned rows
Two different gates must have identical polynomials
The witness must be unique for a given set of public inputs
questions.explanation: Copy constraints tie cells together so that the proof enforces they stay equal.

questions.question: If you assign the same integer to two cells but never add an equality constraint between them, what is true in the proof system?
options: They are not logically linked; the prover could change one without affecting the other as long as all enabled gates still pass
They are automatically linked because they were assigned the same integer
They are linked only if they are in the same column
They are linked only if they are in the same row
questions.explanation: Assignments are just witness values; only constraints (like equality constraints) make relationships provable.

questions.question: Consider the vanishing-product range check ∏_{v in allowed} (x - v) = 0. When does it hold?
options: Exactly when x equals one of the allowed values (in the field)
Exactly when x is not in the allowed set
Only when x equals the last allowed value
Only when the allowed set is empty
questions.explanation: The product is zero iff one factor is zero, which happens when x matches some allowed value.

questions.question: In Halo2 terms, which pairing best matches configure vs synthesize?
options: Configure declares columns + constraints; synthesize assigns witness values and enables selectors
Configure assigns witness values; synthesize generates the proving key
Configure verifies the proof; synthesize creates the transcript
Configure chooses the curve; synthesize picks the hash function
questions.explanation: Configuration sets up the constraint system; synthesis fills the table with concrete witness assignments.

questions.question: Attack mindset: what can go wrong if a required selector is never enabled on any row?
options: The intended constraint is never enforced, so a prover may produce a proof for an invalid statement
The circuit becomes constant-time, which breaks soundness
The field modulus becomes public, which breaks zero knowledge
The prover is forced to reveal the witness values
questions.explanation: If q(row)=0 everywhere, then q(row)*t(row)=0 holds trivially, so the gate provides no soundness.
